## Base Case: The Three State Model on The Complete Phylogeny

Let's load some useful libraries and some simulated data for 100 sites.
<style>
    img {
        border: 0;
    }
</style>
```{r load_lib_object}
library(ape)
library(data.table)
library(memento)

data("object")
str(object)
```

Followed by a bit of data cleaning...

```{r clean}
meth_mtx <- object$MF + object$MR
unmeth_mtx <- object$UF + object$UR
colnames(meth_mtx) <- colnames(unmeth_mtx) <- object$tree$tip.label
chr_pos_object <- paste0(object$details$Chrom, "_", object$details$Pos)
rownames(meth_mtx) <- rownames(unmeth_mtx) <- chr_pos_object

df_meta <- object$meta
filters <- object$filter.param
dt_annotation <- data.table(object$details)
dt_annotation[, chr_pos := paste0(Chrom, "_", Pos)]
setkey(dt_annotation, chr_pos)

tree <- object$tree
tree$tip.label <- gsub("PD40521_Normal_EM1_", "", tree$tip.label)
colnames(meth_mtx) <- colnames(unmeth_mtx) <- gsub("PD40521_Normal_EM1_", "", 
                                                   colnames(unmeth_mtx))
range(tree$edge.length)
```

The tree's branch lengths are in units of years (the individual's age). Memento allows you to input trees with branch lengths in units of years or number of SNVs. If the latter is true, set the boolean Memento setting tree_branch_is_snv to TRUE. Ensure the tree does not contain zero-length branches and convert the bifurcating tree to a polytomous one.

```{r rescale_poly, out.width="700px", out.height="700px", dpi = 300, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, fig.fullwidth=TRUE}
tree_di <- tree
if(any(tree$edge.length == 0)){
  tree <- di2multi(tree) # convert to polytomy
}
tree
{par(mar=rep(1, 4))
  plot.phylo(tree)
  nodelabels(cex = 0.6)
  edgelabels(cex = 0.6)}
```

Some labels at the top of the tree are overlapping. Let's see what a tree in which each branch length is 1 unit long looks like.

```{r plot_unit, out.width="700px", out.height="700px", dpi = 300, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, fig.fullwidth=TRUE}
unit_tree <- tree
unit_tree$edge.length <- rep(1, length(unit_tree$edge.length))
{par(mar=rep(1, 4))
  plot.phylo(unit_tree)
  nodelabels(cex = 0.8)
  edgelabels(cex = 0.8)}
```

That's better.

Here, we'll be working with the three state model. The three states are demethylated, half-methylated and methylated, which corresponds to 0, 0.5 and 1 methlyated read fraction, respectively. The fraction is computed by dividing the number of methlyated reads by the total number of reads at that site. As there are 3 states, there are 9 possible transitions.
To change the settings to a four state model, run set_memento_settings(new_number_of_states = 4).

```{r settings}
settings <- memento_settings()
settings
```

The table below shows which state each transition starts from (row) and ends at (column).

```{r echo=FALSE, results='asis', fig.align = 'left'}
states_mtx <- settings[["state_transition_mtx"]]
new_names <- paste0(dimnames(states_mtx)[[1]], c(" (0)", " (0.5)", " (1)"))
dimnames(states_mtx) <- list(new_names, new_names)

knitr::kable(states_mtx, position = "left", align = "ccc", "html") #%>%
  # kableExtra::kable_styling(position = "left", full_width = F) %>%
  # kableExtra::column_spec(1, bold = T) %>%
  # kableExtra::row_spec(0, background = "white")
```

Let's find changes. First we compute the priors, which are the probabilities of each expected tip state vector. We set m to 2, meaning we will find up to 2 independent changes on the phylogeny. We set n_top_br to 2, meaning we ask for best two assignments to be returned.

```{r find_changes_full}
priors <- generate_priors(full_tree = tree, 
                          m = 2)
# find changes
assignments_full <- compute_probabilities3(priors_per_tree = priors,
                                     m_reads_matrix = meth_mtx,
                                     u_reads_matrix = unmeth_mtx, 
                                     n_top_br = 2,
                                     ro = 0.95, 
                                     verbose = TRUE)
head(assignments_full, 10)

```

Great, we have found state changes for each site. The columns only_branch, starting_state and branch_state show which branches changed, the starting state at the root node and which transitions the branches underwent, respectively. The column probability contains the probability of given state changes.

Columns that start with "ss_" contain the sum of branch lengths, which start in each possible state (here 1, 2 or 3, which correspond to demethylated, half-methylated and methylated, respectively), while columns that start with "nt_" show the number of transitions of each type that occurred in that assignment. These columns are used for estimating rates.

In the first row, the most likely assignment for this position is "n", which means "no change" so the root and tip states are the same. The starting state is inferred to be in state 2 (half-methylated) and branch changes are of type 5 (the transition is from state 0.5 to 0.5). This assignment has a probability of 80%. The second row reports the second most likely assignment for this position and has a probability of 7%.

Position 1_12 (9th row) is most likely to have changed on branch 58. The root starting state is 3 (i.e. 1 or methylated) and the branch underwent transition 7, which is a change from 1 to 0.

Let's see what these assignments actually look like. We're only interested in the best solution so we'll filter the others out.

```{r hm_full, out.width="700px", out.height="700px", dpi = 300, fig.height=10, fig.width=10, fig.fullwidth=TRUE}
rate_mtx <- meth_mtx/(meth_mtx + unmeth_mtx)

assignments_best <- assignments_full[rank == 1,]

some_assignments <- c("n.3:9", "58.3:7","29_58.1:2_3", "2_17.2:4_3", "18_30.3:7_8", 
                      "32_35.2:6_8", "31_36.2:6_7", "4_30.3:8_8")

for(i in 1:length(some_assignments)){
  hm_plot <- plot_heatmap(assignment = some_assignments[i],
                          full_dt = assignments_best,
                          meth_rate_mtx = rate_mtx,
                          tree = tree)
  plot(hm_plot)
}

```

## Advanced Case: Splitting the Phylogeny

In some heatmaps, it seems like additional changes occurred but since we only allow up to 2 changes, these aren't picked up. This tree has 30 branches, which is quite a lot, so if we allow more than 3 independent changes, computing the priors will be time (and memory) consuming. To avoid this, we can split the tree into smaller subtrees, and find changes to each subtree. Allowing 3 changes per subtree across 2 subtrees, we can find up to 6 changes on the full tree (2 subtrees * 3 changes per subtree). The function divide_tree_into_subtrees() takes the complete tree and finds internal nodes, which have an appropriate number of descendants (appropriate meaning within size limits set by the user), and returns their subtrees along with the root tree, which is the top level tree (its root is the root of the complete tree) that will now have new tips that represent roots of subtrees. The total number of branches across all subtrees will equal the number of branches in the complete phylogeny.

```{r, error=TRUE}
subtrees <- divide_tree_into_subtrees(full_tree = tree, max_subtree_size = 15)
```

Sometimes, the tree doesn't fall apart into subtrees *nicely*. Try to play around with various cutoffs (aim for between 5 and 20 tips per subtree), or you can provide a list of custom nodes to use as subtree roots. This requires manual inspection of the tree and hand picking the nodes.

```{r}
subtrees <- divide_tree_into_subtrees(full_tree = tree, max_subtree_size = 12)
subtrees_custom <- divide_tree_into_subtrees(full_tree = tree, custom_nodes = c(47, 33))
```

Yay, this worked. Let's see what these look like.

```{r plot_subtrees, fig.align = "center", out.width="700px", out.height="700px", dpi = 300, fig.height=10, fig.width=10, fig.fullwidth=TRUE}
j <- rep(c(1:3), each = 2)
cex_val <- 1.5
par(mfrow = c(3, 2),
    mar = c(1, 1, 1, 1))
for(i in 1:6){
  my_tree <- subtrees[[j[i]]]
  if(i %% 2 == 0){
    my_tree_unit <- my_tree
    my_tree_unit$edge.length <- rep(1, length(my_tree_unit$edge.length))
    {plot.phylo(my_tree_unit, main = names(subtrees)[j[i]], cex = cex_val)
      nodelabels(cex = cex_val)
      edgelabels(cex = cex_val)}
  }else{
    {plot.phylo(my_tree, main = names(subtrees)[j[i]], cex = cex_val)
      nodelabels(cex = cex_val)
      edgelabels(cex = cex_val)}
  }
}

```

Nice. Let's compute the priors and find changes on each subtree.

```{r priors_sub}
# compute priors
priors_p_subtree <- generate_priors(all_trees = subtrees, full_tree = tree)

# find changes on each subtree
assignments <- lapply(priors_p_subtree,
                      compute_probabilities3, 
                      m_reads_matrix = meth_mtx,
                      u_reads_matrix = unmeth_mtx, 
                      ro = 0.95, 
                      verbose = TRUE)
head(assignments[[1]])
```

This is a table of changes found on the first subtree. But branches are numbered relative to the subtree root, so we have to find which branch on the full tree they would correspond to.

```{r}
# find candidate changes on the full tree
converted_dt <- convert_sub_to_full_tree_branches(assignments = assignments,
                                                  subtrees = subtrees,
                                                  full_tree = tree)
head(converted_dt)
```

Sweet, the combined branch column shows which branches might have changed on the full tree. These were obtained per subtree and since each subtree can have a different starting state, we do not know which state transitions happened on each branch. We also do not know the probability of given branch changes on the full tree.

We would like to get a parsimonious solution for the full tree, where we will know the most likely starting state at root, which branches changed and which states they transitioned from and to, along with the solution's probability. To obtain this, we permute the candidate branches on the full tree and estimate their probability. We start with the full set (including all candidate changes) and a leave-one-out set. If the smaller set contains the most probable solution, we estimate the probability for a set that drops another branch, repeating the process until the not-smallest set contains the solution.

```{r, find_set}
mle_branch_dt <- find_most_likely_set(dt_pre =  converted_dt,
                                      full_tree = tree,
                                      ro = 0.95,
                                      n_top_br = 2,
                                      m_mtx = meth_mtx,
                                      u_mtx = unmeth_mtx,
                                      fraction_estimate = 1,
                                      verbose = FALSE,
                                      dt_anno = dt_annotation)
head(mle_branch_dt)
```

Nice, we obtained the best two solutions for each site. 

Let's see what these changes look like and compare new assignments to the original ones made on the full tree.

```{r}
mle_dt_best <- mle_branch_dt[rank == 1,]
same_sites_as_before <- assignments_best[branch %in% some_assignments][["chr_pos"]] # filter to plotted positions
mle_subset <- mle_dt_best[chr_pos %in% same_sites_as_before]
mle_subset[, .(probability, branch, only_branch, starting_state, branch_state, n_assignments_mle)]
```

We found some additional changes! Let's plot these.

```{r plot_hm_split, out.width="700px", out.height="700px", dpi = 300, fig.height=10, fig.width=10, fig.fullwidth=TRUE}
same_sites_new_assignment <- names(sort(table(mle_subset[["branch"]]), decreasing = TRUE))

for(i in 1:length(same_sites_new_assignment)){
  hm_plot_split <- plot_heatmap(assignment = same_sites_new_assignment[i],
                       full_dt = mle_subset,
                       meth_rate_mtx = rate_mtx,
                       tree = tree)
  plot(hm_plot_split)
}
```

These look better than assignments made using the full tree. We picked up some additional changes and the new probabilities of assignments are higher too.
